query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post-synthesis low‐temperature annealing treatment that promotes targeted solute segregation at the internal lamellar colony boundaries of eutectic high-entropy alloys will enhance boundary cohesion, thereby delaying microcrack initiation and simultaneously increasing tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies having unmodified internal boundaries
generation.intervention: Post-synthesis low‐temperature annealing aimed at inducing beneficial solute segregation at internal boundaries
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion due to targeted solute segregation along the lamellar colony interfaces
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment alters the local interfacial chemistry by segregating select solute atoms at internal boundaries, thereby strengthening these interfaces and delaying the nucleation and propagation of microcracks. This integrated effect is expected to improve both tensile strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit higher tensile strength and improved ductility compared to the untreated baseline alloy due to reinforced internal boundaries.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys with unmodified dual-phase lamellar colonies
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated in eutectic HEAs with clearly defined dual-phase lamellar microstructures; the improvement is contingent on optimizing the annealing temperature and duration to achieve solute segregation without detrimental overaging.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in strength and ductility remains uncertain and may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate identical samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies. Subject one set to the proposed low-temperature annealing treatment and retain a control set under conventional processing. Perform room-temperature tensile tests alongside microstructural characterization (using TEM and atom probe tomography) to evaluate the extent of solute segregation and interfacial cohesion.
measurements: Interfacial chemistry and cohesion metrics via TEM/APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and ductility, or if microstructural analyses fail to confirm enhanced solute segregation at internal boundaries compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Meanwhile, due to large residual stress in the fractured Hf0.5 alloy sample, the resolution rate of the EBSD of the lateral surface was extremely low. Therefore, the corresponding EBSD map of the Hf0.5 alloy is not provided in Figure 7. Based on its microstructure (Figure 2a), it can be inferred that the Hf-rich phases at grain boundaries and phase boundaries would pin grain and phase boundaries to delay the initiation and propagation of grain boundary and phase boundary cracks during high-temperature deformation, which was consistent with the phenomenon observed on the cross-section of the Hf0.5 alloy (Figure 8b), ensuring excellent tensile ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
